solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A raised hand

parts.note: surface reading: a single hand put up, as by a pupil wanting to ask a question; setter's reading: a 'hand' is a round of applause, and this one is given by an audience that has risen to its feet

explanation.surface: A pupil puts a hand up in class.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'give someone a big hand' is to applaud them; when the whole audience stands to do it, the hand has been raised.
explanation.definitionFit: Applause delivered by a crowd on its feet is the ultimate show of approval, a 'hand' lifted to standing height.

clue.text: Modern business setting? No

parts.note: surface reading: the up-to-date premises or environment in which a firm operates; setter's reading: the sun is not setting but coming up, so the new kind of business is named after the opposite of sunset

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether this is a modern business setting and is told it is not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setting' looks like a noun for surroundings; read it as the sun setting, and 'No' turns it into the sun coming up.
explanation.definitionFit: A new, fast-growing sector of the economy is called this, by contrast with a declining 'sunset' one.

clue.text: Living nearby, fed by tree and vegetables

indicators.note: fed by means the other pieces are put into the middle

parts.note: around means nearby, as in hanging around

indicators.note: and simply sets the vegetables after the tree inside the holder

parts.note: the bo is the sacred fig tree of Buddhism
veg is short for vegetables

explanation.surface: Someone resident close by, nourished by fruit and greens from their garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Living' looks like residing, but it means alive; the bo is the sacred fig of Buddhism.
explanation.definitionFit: Being above ground, not yet buried, is an idiomatic way of saying still alive.

clue.text: Very bright party clothes always girl's skirts

indicators.note: clothes means the party word dresses the other pieces, wrapping round them

parts.note: a do is a party
ay, or aye, is an old word for always

indicators.note: skirts means just the edges, the first and last letters, of girl

parts.note: read as the word girl, whose first and last letters are taken

explanation.surface: A partygoer's outfit, always loud, worn by a girl with skirts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clothes' is a verb here, not a noun; ay is an old word for always.
explanation.definitionFit: Day-Glo is a brand of fluorescent paint, so the word means glaringly vivid.

clue.text: Fool, single, in Gotham

indicators.note: in places one item inside another, here the word for single within the city named after it

parts.note: Gotham is a nickname for New York, abbreviated NY
an odd sock or glove is a single one without its partner

explanation.surface: A lone fool turns up in Batman's city of Gotham.
explanation.walkthrough: Gotham suggests Batman's villains, but it is the old nickname for New York.
explanation.definitionFit: A noddy is an old word for a simpleton or silly person, one who nods off or nods along.

clue.text: Risky? Possibly not for one about to accept caution

indicators.note: 'to accept' has the outer letters take in the word for caution
'possibly' says the word not could be arranged another way
'about' turns the abbreviation for 'for one' back to front

parts.note: EG, short for exempli gratia, means 'for example', i.e. for one
to heed is to take care; heed as a noun means caution or attention

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a person about to be cautioned is really in a risky position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges NOT into ONT; 'about' turns EG round to GE; 'to accept' puts HEED between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the edge means being in a precarious, dangerous state, so risky fits as an adjective.

clue.text: A metaphor about fashionable drug

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for metaphor wraps around the word for fashionable

parts.note: a trope is a figure of speech, a metaphor being one
in means in fashion

explanation.surface: A writer reaches for a metaphor about a trendy drug.
explanation.definitionFit: Atropine is a poisonous alkaloid from deadly nightshade, used medically to dilate pupils and steady heart rate.

clue.text: Murder is evil, but not very

indicators.note: but not asks for something to be left out, here the abbreviation for very

parts.note: vice is wickedness or evil
v is the standard abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: A moral pronouncement: killing is wicked, though perhaps not especially so.
explanation.definitionFit: To ice someone is gangster slang for killing them.

clue.text: General waiting for conscription

parts.note: national means general, affecting the whole country
waiting at table is service

explanation.surface: An army general is waiting for the call-up to begin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General' looks like an officer, but it is an adjective meaning nationwide.
explanation.definitionFit: National service was Britain's compulsory military service for young men, ended in 1960: conscription by another name.

clue.text: Sex never good? That's unknown

parts.note: no as in 'no way', never
OK means all right, good
y is one of the algebraic unknowns

explanation.surface: Someone claims never to have had good sex, a thing they say they know nothing of.
explanation.definitionFit: Nooky is jokey slang for sexual intercourse.

clue.text: Cleaner put man off

indicators.note: 'off' completes the phrasal verb 'put off' after the word for man has been placed, so the pieces simply follow on

parts.note: with the 'off' at the clue's end, put (off) means deter, to discourage
a gent is a gentleman, a man

explanation.surface: Someone's cleaning lady was put off by a man.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'put off' is split, with 'man' sitting in the middle, but the pieces are simply joined: DETER then GENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A detergent is a cleaning agent, a substance used to wash things.

clue.text: I waste time conserving energy in the best way

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: conserving means keeping something safely within, so the time-wasting verb holds the letter for energy

parts.note: to dally is to dawdle, wasting time
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: An idler admits to wasting time while saving energy, which is the perfect approach.
explanation.definitionFit: Ideally means in a perfect way, as things would go under the best possible circumstances.

clue.text: Grass and earth break up in well

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for earth

indicators.note: in puts one piece inside another, here the words for break up inside the word for well

parts.note: so, as in 'so, what now?', can stand for well
to part is to separate or break up

explanation.surface: Grass and soil come apart inside a well shaft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well' is not a water source but the word used to start a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Esparto is a tough Spanish and North African grass used for making paper, rope and baskets.

clue.text: An adult should be this guilty

definitions.meaning: first meaning: sensible and trustworthy, as grown-ups are meant to be
second meaning: to blame for something

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a grown-up who should feel guilt; the two halves are two senses of the same adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means both reliable and mature and also accountable or culpable for a wrong.

clue.text: Almost primitive nobleman

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter of the word for primitive is dropped

parts.note: early, as in early man, means primitive

explanation.surface: A nobleman is described as close to a caveman.
explanation.definitionFit: An earl is a British peer ranking above a viscount and below a marquess.

clue.text: Insist on bombing bridges with a rebel

indicators.note: something that has been bombed is blown apart, so the letters of insist are scattered and rebuilt
a bridge spans something, so the scrambled letters stretch over and around the word for with

parts.note: the letters of insist rearranged
and means along with
taken as written

explanation.surface: A guerrilla demands that bridges be blown up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bombing bridges' reads as a demolition plan; 'on bombing' scrambles insist and 'bridges' is a verb for spanning.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sandinistas were the left-wing rebels who overthrew Nicaragua's Somoza regime in 1979.

clue.text: Very high up in jumbo, miss it landing

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the hidden letters are read from bottom to top
in says the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

parts.note: the run from the last letter of jumbo to the first two of landing

explanation.surface: Up high in a jumbo jet, someone hopes not to miss the landing.
explanation.definitionFit: Altissimo is the musical term for the very highest register, above altissimo's lower neighbour alto.

clue.text: Cut caused by spike leading to charge

parts.note: to spike or lace a drink is to add alcohol or a drug to it secretly
a rate is a price or charge

explanation.surface: A wound inflicted by a sharp spike leads to a criminal charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading to' simply places the first piece before the second.
explanation.definitionFit: To lacerate is to tear or gash flesh, so it means to cut.

clue.text: "We" are not "us" — "us" is wrong

indicators.note: if something is wrong it is not in proper order, so the letters before need rearranging

parts.note: every letter of these words, with the quotation marks and dash ignored

explanation.surface: A grammatical quibble: 'we' is not the same word as 'us', so using 'us' is incorrect.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is French, literally 'we others', used to mean 'we ourselves' or 'people like us'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nous autres is a French phrase for 'we', stressing the group as opposed to others, sometimes borrowed into English.

clue.text: Crash party with Nazi bodyguard

parts.note: a do is a party
the SS was Hitler's elite guard

explanation.surface: Someone gatecrashes a party alongside Hitler's guards.
explanation.walkthrough: To doss is British slang for sleeping rough or on someone's floor.
explanation.definitionFit: To crash, in slang, is to sleep somewhere makeshift for the night, which is exactly what dossing means.

clue.text: From crew — it's an enemy aircraft

parts.note: a band is a group or crew of people
taken as written

explanation.surface: A member of an aircrew spots a hostile plane.
explanation.definitionFit: Bandit is RAF and pilots' slang for a hostile aircraft, as in 'bandits at two o'clock'.

clue.text: First part of doctors and nurses involved nudity

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so the letters are mixed into a new order
the first part of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: The children's game of doctors and nurses led to some getting their clothes off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' rearranges D plus NURSES. Doctors and nurses is a childish game of pretend examination.
explanation.definitionFit: Undress as a noun means a state of being unclothed or partly clothed, hence nakedness.

clue.text: This is read out before beginning to read

definitions.text: This is read out before beginning to read

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or wrong, so the letters of is read are reshuffled

parts.note: these six letters rearranged

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only the first of read is used

parts.note: the first letter of the final word

explanation.surface: Something gets read aloud before the reading proper starts.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: the salutation is what you read first, before the body of a letter begins.
explanation.definitionFit: The formal greeting opening a business letter is the first thing read, ahead of the message itself.

clue.text: Briefly protest about one's belief

indicators.note: about means around, so the shortened protest wraps the next piece
briefly means cut short, so the last letter of the word for protest goes

parts.note: a demo is a protest march
one is I, plus the 's taken as is

explanation.surface: Someone protests briefly about their own faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' reads as a possessive, but gives the numeral I and the contraction for is.
explanation.definitionFit: Deism is a religious position: belief in a creator God who does not intervene in the world.

clue.text: Conductor to study in Italy

parts.note: taken as written
to scan is to examine or study closely
taken as written
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: A music conductor goes to study in Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Arturo Toscanini was the celebrated Italian conductor who led La Scala and the NBC Symphony Orchestra.

clue.text: Very posh, but not much money

parts.note: so means very, as in 'so kind'
U means upper-class, from the old 'U and non-U' classification of speech

explanation.surface: Someone is terribly upper-class yet nearly broke.
explanation.definitionFit: A sou was an old French coin of tiny value, so 'not a sou' means having almost no cash.

clue.text: Name capital city on peninsula

parts.note: to dub someone is to give them a name
A1 means first-rate or capital, written with the letter I for the digit

explanation.surface: A quiz asks for the capital of a city-state on a peninsula.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' tempts you towards a seat of government, but here it is the old exclamation of approval, meaning excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Dubai is the largest city of the United Arab Emirates, on the Arabian Peninsula.

clue.text: I don't know passenger's last words?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an admission of being stumped by a question
second meaning: what a traveller might say to the driver on arriving at the destination

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second reading, taking 'got me there' as 'brought me to my destination'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom concedes you cannot answer, and read literally it thanks a driver for delivering you.
